# Ezekiel 25 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

Ezekiel 25 opens a new major section of the book (chs. 25–32): oracles of judgment against foreign nations. After chapters 4–24 pronounced judgment on Judah and Jerusalem, and before chapters 33–48 promise future restoration for Israel, these oracles demonstrate that God holds all nations accountable — not only His covenant people. The chapter addresses four nations surrounding Judah: Ammon (vv. 1–7), Moab (vv. 8–11), Edom (vv. 12–14), and the Philistines (vv. 15–17). All four are condemned for gloating over Jerusalem's fall and mistreating God's people. — Constable, StudyLight.org (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-25.html)

Ezekiel addresses seven nations in total (Ammon, Moab, Edom, Philistia, Tyre, Sidon, Egypt), a "perfect number" implying completeness of God's judgment on the heathen world. Remarkably, Babylon is omitted because Ezekiel and Jeremiah understood Babylon as God's instrument of judgment; to resist Babylon was to resist God's will. — Guzik, EnduringWord.com (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-25/); Keil & Delitzsch, StudyLight.org (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-25.html)

The four messages in this chapter each follow a four-part pattern: introduction, indictment, punishment, and outcome. The refrain "then you/they will know that I am the LORD" closes each oracle. — Constable (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-25.html)

---

## VERSES 1–2: The Call to Prophesy against Ammon

**v. 1 — "Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying…"**

This begins a new section after the prophet had completed his messages to the Jews. Ezekiel, still in Babylon, is now directed to prophesy against the Gentiles, beginning with those nearest to Judah. — Gill, StudyLight.org (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-25.html)

**v. 2 — "Son of man, set your face against the Ammonites and prophesy against them."**

"Set your face" means to adopt a determined, frowning, menacing stance — to look boldly toward Ammon with a message of judgment. The Ammonites were descendants of Lot (through his younger daughter, Genesis 19:38) and implacable enemies of Israel who hated their religion and envied their prosperity. — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-25.html); Ellicott notes their long history of hostility: they joined Moab against Israel under Eglon (Judges 3:13), fought cruelly against Saul (1 Samuel 11:2-11), warred against David (2 Samuel 10), and had recently occupied the vacant cities of Gad (Jeremiah 49:1). — Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-25.html)

---

## VERSES 3–5: The Indictment and Punishment of Ammon

**v. 3 — "Because you exclaimed, 'Aha!' when My sanctuary was profaned, when the land of Israel was laid waste, and when the house of Judah went into exile…"**

The Ammonites' sin was gloating — they said "Aha!" (an expression of malicious joy) over three calamities: (1) the profanation/desecration of the temple, (2) the desolation of the land of Israel (the northern kingdom, already destroyed by Assyria), and (3) the exile of Judah (the southern kingdom, taken by Babylon). Their joy was not merely political but explicitly religious — they rejoiced at the destruction of God's sanctuary. — Guzik (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-25/); Gill notes this was "brutish and barbarous behaviour" showing they hated Israel's worship and took delight in the ruin of their neighbours. — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-25.html)

According to Ezekiel 21:18-20, Nebuchadnezzar had set out against both Judah and Ammon; Ammon apparently capitulated and turned against Judah. — Guzik, citing Feinberg

**v. 4 — "Therefore I will indeed give you as a possession to the people of the East. They will set up their camps and pitch their tents among you. They will eat your fruit and drink your milk."**

"The people of the East" (literally "sons of the east") refers to nomadic desert tribes — Bedouins, or possibly the Chaldeans/Babylonians, Medes and Persians, or Arabians. Gill notes Jewish commentators Jarchi and Kimchi identified them as Chaldeans/Syrians or Medes/Persians, but "the men of the east" commonly refers to Arabians. — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-25.html)

Ellicott clarifies that these nomads would be the *possessors*, not necessarily the *conquerors*; Nebuchadnezzar did the conquering, but the Bedouins would subsequently occupy and settle the land, living in tents, consuming the produce. — Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-25.html)

**v. 5 — "I will make Rabbah a pasture for camels, and Ammon a resting place for sheep. Then you will know that I am the LORD."**

Rabbah was the royal city, the only important town of the Ammonites (later rebuilt as Philadelphia by Ptolemy Philadelphus, and today the site of Amman, Jordan). The prophecy that it would become a "stable for camels" (lit. a pasture/couching-place) has been strikingly fulfilled: the Bedouins use the ruins for their flocks. Travellers report "lonely desolation in a rich country" as the characteristic of the area. — Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-25.html); Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-25.html)

"Then you will know that I am the LORD": This refrain throughout the chapter refers not to a penitent conversion but to an inescapable recognition of God's power through experiencing His wrath. — Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-25.html); Guzik (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-25/)

---

## VERSES 6–7: Expanded Guilt and Judgment of Ammon

**v. 6 — "Because you clapped your hands and stomped your feet and rejoiced over the land of Israel with a heart full of contempt…"**

The sin first mentioned in v. 3 is now enlarged. Clapping hands and stamping feet were gestures of intense joy and malicious glee (cf. Isaiah 55:12). Their outward gestures revealed an inner "heart full of contempt" (or "despite"/disdain). The Ammonites demonstrated "the wretched malignity of their dispositions" — they hated Israel with a perfect hatred. — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-25.html); Guzik notes their sin was "religious mockery" — they rejoiced over God's sanctuary, not just a political rival. — Guzik (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-25/)

**v. 7 — "Therefore I will indeed stretch out My hand against you and give you as plunder to the nations. I will cut you off from the peoples and exterminate you from the countries. I will destroy you, and you will know that I am the LORD."**

In just retaliation for their clapping hands, God would stretch out *His* hand — "a heavy one" — against them. "Give you as plunder" (or "for meat/food," as some Hebrew texts read) means to be devoured and consumed by the nations. They would cease to exist as a distinct people or country, cut off from among the nations. — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-25.html)

Historically, the Ammonites were absorbed by the Arabs and their name disappeared from history. — Guzik, citing Feinberg (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-25/); Constable adds that after Nebuchadnezzar destroyed Ammon, Bedouins from the east plundered it. — Constable (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-25.html)

---

## VERSES 8–11: Judgment on Moab (and Seir)

**v. 8 — "Because Moab and Seir said, 'Look, the house of Judah is like all the other nations'…"**

Moab and Seir (Edom) are mentioned together before being treated separately (Moab in vv. 8–11, Edom in vv. 12–14). Moab descended from Lot's incest with his elder daughter (Genesis 19:37); Seir was a mountain region of the Edomites, descendants of Esau. Both were "cousins" to Israel. — Guzik (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-25/)

Their taunt — "Judah is like all the other nations" — was a direct assault on Yahweh Himself. They claimed that Judah's special status as God's covenant people was a sham; if Judah fell like every other nation, then her God was no different from Chemosh or any other deity. The Mesha Stone (Moabite Stone) records king Mesha's boast that Chemosh had vanquished Israel. — Guzik, citing Block and Alexander (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-25/); Gill notes they said this "blasphemously" — where is the God they boasted of? — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-25.html)

**v. 9 — "Therefore I will indeed expose the flank of Moab beginning with its frontier cities—Beth-jeshimoth, Baal-meon, and Kiriathaim—the glory of the land."**

"Expose the flank" (or "open the shoulder") means to lay the country open to invasion at its strongest point, its frontier defences. The three named cities were all north of the Arnon River — territory that had belonged to Israel (the tribe of Reuben) before Moab reconquered it. Ellicott suggests they are named as the rightful possession of Israel, making them the fitting starting point for judgment. — Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-25.html)

Beth-jeshimoth was in the Jordan Valley guarding the eastern ascent; Baal-meon lay further east in northern Moab; Kiriathaim ("the double city") was on the Medeba Plateau — its name means "the glory of the land," creating a wordplay with the phrase in the verse. — Constable (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-25.html)

**v. 10 — "I will give it along with the Ammonites as a possession to the people of the East, so that the Ammonites will no longer be remembered among the nations."**

Moab would share Ammon's fate — handed over to the same "people of the East." The phrase "along with the Ammonites" (or "against the Ammonites," as the Targum reads) means the same eastern invaders who destroyed Ammon would enter Moab and possess it. Both nations would cease to be remembered. — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-25.html); Ellicott notes the nations were so closely connected that what was said of one applied to the other. — Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-25.html)

**v. 11 — "So I will execute judgments on Moab, and they will know that I am the LORD."**

Though the Chaldeans and Arabians were the instruments, the destruction was from the Lord — it was His hand, His vengeance. The purpose was self-revelation: that Moab would know that Yahweh, the God of Israel, is the true God. — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-25.html)

---

## VERSES 12–14: Judgment on Edom

**v. 12 — "Because Edom acted vengefully against the house of Judah, and in so doing incurred grievous guilt…"**

Edom's distinctive sin was *vengeance*. The phrase is literally "revenging with revenge" — an unrelieved, unabated revenge. The Edomites, descended from Esau, bore an ancient grudge going back to Jacob's taking of the birthright and blessing, and later to David's subjugation of Edom. When Jerusalem fell, they not only rejoiced but actively helped the Babylonians, urged them to greater cruelty, and waylaid fleeing Jews to cut them off (cf. Psalm 137:7; Obadiah 1:11; Ezekiel 35:5). — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-25.html); Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-25.html); Guzik (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-25/)

**v. 13 — "I will stretch out My hand against Edom and cut off from it both man and beast. I will make it a wasteland, and from Teman to Dedan they will fall by the sword."**

God's judgment would be comprehensive: both "man and beast" would be cut off — either by sword, famine, pestilence, or plague. "From Teman to Dedan" is like saying "from Dan to Beersheba" for Israel: the entire country, south to north, would be devastated. Teman (meaning "south") was a southern district famous for its wisdom (Jeremiah 49:7); Dedan lay in the north. — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-25.html); Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-25.html); Constable (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-25.html)

**v. 14 — "I will take My vengeance on Edom by the hand of My people Israel, and they will deal with Edom according to My anger and wrath."**

This is a distinctive element: unlike Ammon and Moab (judged by the "people of the East"), Edom would be judged specifically *by the hand of My people Israel*. Ellicott sees this fulfilled when John Hyrcanus (a Jewish Maccabean leader) conquered the Idumeans (Edomites), compelled them to submit to circumcision, and absorbed them into the Jewish people. After Herod (himself an Idumean) reigned as king of the Jews, the name "Edom" disappeared from history. — Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-25.html)

Gill also sees fulfillment in the Maccabees (1 Maccabees 5:3; Josephus Antiquities 13.9.1) but notes that some, like Kimchi, understood this as yet future — to be fulfilled in the times of the Messiah. — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-25.html)

Guzik sees the principle that God can deploy His own people as instruments of His justice, though He will lay aside such instruments if they exceed His purpose. — Guzik (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-25/)

**"Then they will know My vengeance"** — this knowing is not salvific; it is the experiential knowledge of God's wrath so unmistakable that they cannot deny His power and justice. — Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-25.html)

---

## VERSES 15–17: Judgment on the Philistines

**v. 15 — "Because the Philistines acted in vengeance, taking vengeance with malice of soul to destroy Judah with ancient hostility…"**

The Philistines were ancient, implacable enemies of Israel — not blood relatives like Ammon, Moab, and Edom, but Mediterranean "Sea Peoples" from the Aegean who settled the coastal strip of Canaan. Their hostility ran from the time of the Judges (Samson), through Saul and David, to the time of Ahaz (2 Chronicles 28:18) and likely at Jerusalem's fall. They acted "with malice of soul" (a despiteful/spiteful heart) and "ancient hostility" (or "perpetual hatred"). — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-25.html); Constable (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-25.html)

Gill notes they were taking revenge for past defeats — Goliath's death, David's conquests, the burning of their images. Their hatred was "old" and "perpetual." — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-25.html)

**v. 16 — "Behold, I will stretch out My hand against the Philistines, and I will cut off the Cherethites and destroy the remnant along the coast."**

The "Cherethites" (or Cherethim) were a Philistine group living on the southern coast (1 Samuel 30:14; Zephaniah 2:5). Their name may be related to "Cretans," indicating origin from Crete. The Hebrew contains a striking wordplay: *"I will cut off [hikrati] the Cherethites [keretim]"* — "I will cut off the cutters-off" or "I will slay the slayers." — Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-25.html); Guzik, citing Feinberg (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-25/)

The "remnant along the coast" refers to those Philistine cities (Ashdod, Ashkelon, etc.) that had survived earlier judgments — even the remnant would be destroyed. — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-25.html)

David had a group of Cherethite mercenaries in his own army (2 Samuel 15:18). — Guzik, citing Wright (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-25/)

**v. 17 — "I will execute great vengeance against them with furious reproof. Then they will know that I am the LORD, when I lay My vengeance upon them."**

The Philistines receive the most severe form of judgment in this chapter: no human agent is named. God will punish the Philistines directly — "great vengeance" with "furious rebukes." — Guzik, citing Vawter and Hoppe (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-25/)

Gill notes the retaliation principle: as they acted with vengeance and fury against God's people, so they would receive vengeance and fury from God. The judgments would be "for quantity and quality, very great." The outcome is that they would "know that I am the LORD" — seeing God's hand, acknowledging His justice, and confessing the God of Israel as the only true God. — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-25.html)

## Differences between Protestant Traditions

### Reformed / Presbyterian
The Reformed tradition emphasizes God's sovereignty over all nations. As noted by Ligonier, the recommended Reformed commentators (Block, Duguid, Derek Thomas) stress that these oracles demonstrate the Lord's universal reign and the accountability of all nations — none are outside His jurisdiction. The judgment on the nations is an outworking of the Abrahamic covenant (Genesis 12:3: "I will curse those who curse you"). — Monergism.com (https://www.monergism.com/topics/mp3-audio-multimedia/00-old-testament-sermons-book/ezekiel/ezekiel-%E2%80%94-reformed-sermons-bible-8); Ligonier recommends Iain Duguid's commentary as a "very careful reading of the book from a Reformed perspective." — Ligonier (https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/top-5-commentaries-ezekiel)

Reformed commentator G. Campbell Morgan (cited by Guzik) sees the purpose of judgment as self-revelation: "Those who fail to find Him in the light of His revelation… He brings to know Him through judgment." — Guzik (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-25/)

### Baptist
John Gill, a Particular Baptist, provides extensive historical detail and notes that while judgment falls on these nations as corporate entities, individual descendants may yet have a future (e.g., Jeremiah 49:6 promises eventual restoration for Ammon). His commentary treats the prophecies as literally fulfilled in history through Nebuchadnezzar, the Maccabees, and the Arabs. He is careful to distinguish between the political destruction of nations and the possibility of individual salvation. — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-25.html)

### Lutheran
Keil & Delitzsch (a Lutheran work) highlights the structural significance of the number seven (seven nations, seven prophecies against Egypt) as denoting "the completion of the works of God" — the divine judgment executed and completed upon the heathen world. They also note a distinctive feature of Ezekiel compared to other prophets: Ezekiel does not include promises of ultimate pardon or conversion for these nations (unlike Isaiah and Jeremiah), but stops with the announcement of utter destruction of their earthly and temporal condition. The apparent exception for Egypt (Ezekiel 29:13-16) is only a restoration to a lowly, impotent kingdom that would offer no temptation for Israel to trust in it. — Keil & Delitzsch, StudyLight.org (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-25.html)

(This Lutheran reading stands in some tension with other traditions that see the "know that I am the LORD" refrain as potentially open to eschatological conversion.)

### Anglican
Ellicott's Commentary (Anglican) emphasizes the historical fulfillment through identifiable events: Ammon and Moab destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar and occupied by Bedouins; Edom conquered by John Hyrcanus and absorbed into the Jewish people; the Philistines gradually disappeared. He is careful to note that "knowing the LORD" here is not penitent recognition but experiential acknowledgment of His power through wrath. He also explicitly rejects readings that see in v. 14 an intimation of Edom's ultimate conversion and incorporation into the Church, calling this "quite foreign" to the scope and connection. — Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-25.html)

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)
Guzik emphasizes application for believers: God's judgment on the nations reassures God's people that He sees and will answer hatred, mockery, and vengeance against His own. He focuses on the "self-revelation" purpose of judgment — God wants people to know Him, even if through wrath. He also highlights the structural artistry (seven nations, seven prophecies against Egypt), the Abrahamic covenant background, and the principle from 1 Peter 4:17-18 — if judgment begins with God's household, how much more for the disobedient nations. — Guzik (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-25/)

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship (NET Bible notes / Bible Odyssey)
The NET Bible notes were not directly accessed, but the search results from Constable (who draws on modern scholarship) and the Bridgeway Bible Commentary reflect mainstream evangelical scholarship: the oracles functioned to reassure the exiles that God's justice was universal and that the nations who gloated over Israel's fall would not escape. — Constable (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-25.html)

The Bridgeway Bible Commentary notes that the Philistines' judgment is unique in that "the prophet does not mention any human agent of punishment" — God will pass judgment directly. — Bridgeway, StudyLight.org (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/ezekiel-25.html)

Modern scholarship also notes that Ezekiel's omission of Babylon reflects his and Jeremiah's political stance that Babylon was God's chosen instrument. — Guzik, citing Vawter and Hoppe (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-25/)

### Catholic and Orthodox Readings
I was unable to access specific Catholic or Orthodox commentaries on Ezekiel 25 from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org within the available search limits. The Catholic Encyclopedia (newadvent.org) and similar sources were not returned in searches specific to Ezekiel 25 verse commentary.

### Debated Popular Modern Teaching
No specific prosperity-gospel, Word of Faith, or hyper-grace teachings on Ezekiel 25 were found in the available sources. These movements tend to focus on NT texts and would not typically produce verse-by-verse commentary on Ezekiel 25.

## Key Theological Themes Noted Across Traditions

1. **"Then you/they will know that I am the LORD"** — This refrain closes each oracle. Most commentators agree it does not necessarily indicate saving knowledge or conversion, but the forced recognition of God's power through judgment. — Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-25.html); Guzik (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-25/)

2. **Absence of Babylon** — Ezekiel notably omits Babylon from the oracles. Both Guzik and Keil & Delitzsch see this as intentional: Babylon was God's instrument of judgment, and to resist Babylon was to resist God's will. — Guzik (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-25/); Keil & Delitzsch (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-25.html)

3. **The Abrahamic Covenant** — The judgment of these nations is seen as fulfillment of Genesis 12:3 ("I will bless those who bless you, and whoever curses you I will curse"). Feinberg: "No nation under heaven could touch Israel for ill without bringing down upon them the wrath of almighty God." — Guzik (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-25/)

4. **Edom judged by Israel** — Verse 14 is unique in naming Israel as the agent of judgment. Ellicott sees this fulfilled in John Hyrcanus's conquest (2nd century BC); Gill sees a dual fulfillment in the Maccabees and possibly a future Messianic fulfillment; Guzik sees a principle of God using His people as instruments. — Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-25.html); Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-25.html); Guzik (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-25/)

5. **Contrast with other prophets** — Unlike Isaiah and Jeremiah, Ezekiel does not promise restoration for these nations (except the limited restoration of Egypt in ch. 29). His oracles end with utter destruction. — Keil & Delitzsch (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-25.html)
